idiom_name: private_constant inside the owning module plus one narrow public entry point; private/protected are call-site rules
implementation_notes: Ruby's visibility keywords are runtime call rules, not compile-time grants: private and protected set the visibility of methods (protected meaning callable with a receiver of the same class), and Module#private_constant 'makes a list of existing constants private', so an outside reference to the constant raises NameError (ruby-doc.org, class Module). Neither is checked before the program runs, and both are bypassable at runtime: send steps over method visibility, const_get and module_eval reach private constants, instance_variable_get reads all state. The closest realization is therefore to hold the implementation class in a private constant inside the owning module and expose exactly one public method as the door, accepting that the rest is convention - which is why the file is marked discouraged.
code_sketch:
module Grids
  class Grid                     # implementation
    def recalc(i) = @dirty = i
  end
  private_constant :Grid         # outside references raise NameError

  def self.refresh(id)           # the only public door
    grid_for(id).recalc(0)
  end
end
pitfalls: private_constant hides the name, not the object: Grids.const_get(:Grid) and Module#module_eval still get in, so it prevents mistakes rather than access.
send bypasses private and protected method visibility, and instance_variable_get/set reach any state; protected also leaks easily, since any instance of the same class may call it.

Ruby has no compile step at all, so nothing fails before the program runs: the check happens at the moment of the call, and what the pattern is meant to provide - a grant verified before execution - cannot be provided.
alternative: No compile-time equivalent exists, so use the runtime tools knowingly: hold the implementation in a private constant inside its module (private_constant), expose one narrow public method as the door, and treat private/protected method visibility only as a call-site discipline, because send, const_get, module_eval and instance_variable_get all step over them. Enforce the boundary with linters and review, and when it must actually hold, move the implementation behind a process, a service or a native extension - Ruby cannot fail the program before it runs.
